reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because its primary purpose is an educational case study and implementation tutorial about a Shopify store's reported affiliate-marketing revenue. The affiliate signup, commission tiers, and referral panel are presented as components of the business model, while there is no direct request to transfer money or submit credentials to the creator, and the success disclaimer limits what can be inferred about guaranteed returns.

opening.argument: The video links an unusually large revenue claim to concrete participation steps. Its title foregrounds $1,116,708, while the presenter says viewers can recreate the strategy in their own store. The pathway is not merely theoretical: prospective participants are told to fill out their details, receive affiliate links, and earn commission. That makes the promised income contingent on registration and promotional activity, rather than a neutral discussion of commerce. The presentation also connects the opportunity to customers after purchase, describing follow-up invitations to join affiliate marketing and earn money. A viewer is therefore steered through a simple action-to-income funnel: replicate the model, register, share links, and expect commissions.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this a case study does not remove the solicitation. The reference framing overlooks that the tutorial repeatedly turns the alleged result into an instruction for viewers to reproduce it, and that registration requires personal account details. The absence of a direct transfer to the presenter is not dispositive when the promised benefit is commission income obtained by joining and promoting the program.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted income is affiliate commission tied to referred purchases, not a guaranteed payment for merely registering. The tutorial describes how to configure a store and explicitly presents the material as a case study; it does not establish that viewers will receive the featured revenue or that registration itself produces money. The words about earning commission identify a normal performance condition rather than proof of deception.

opening.argument: Several genuine warning signals appear together: a headline revenue figure of $1,116,708, tiered commissions, and income from recruiting more affiliates. The program is not described as a simple one-level referral code. It offers silver, gold, and platinum levels ranging from 8% to 30%, while the demonstrated structure lets one affiliate recruit others and earn from those affiliates. That combination makes compensation depend on participation in a tiered recruitment network. The presentation emphasizes how powerful and scalable the arrangement is, but the visible and spoken requirements show that advancement and rewards are tied to recruiting and commission thresholds. Those are material characteristics of a recruitment-commission scheme, not merely evidence of ordinary product sales.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference account calls the tiers business components but does not address the decisive feature: commissions can flow from affiliates recruited by another affiliate. Nor does a disclaimer neutralize the structure itself. The combination of prominent revenue, tier progression, and downline commissions is the relevant risk signal, even if the presenter labels the setup optional or discusses it operationally.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The material itself distinguishes ordinary affiliate promotion from the optional multi-level feature: the presenter says he does not endorse or use MLM. Tiered commission rates can describe performance levels without proving downline dependence, and the evidence does not show that viewers must recruit anyone or pay to enter. The existence of a described structure is not by itself proof that the video is deceptive.

opening.argument: The educational packaging functions as a promotional funnel. The presenter does not stop at analyzing a store: he promises the exact setup needed to recreate its success, supplies copy-and-paste templates, and repeatedly explains how to convert buyers into affiliates. He also advises keeping the earning message out of Facebook advertisements while placing smaller prompts on the destination site. That is a deliberate traffic-and-conversion plan designed to recruit participants without presenting the opportunity openly in the initial ad. The case-study format therefore serves promotion: viewers are moved from an attractive product and revenue story to affiliate registration, links, and recruitment. Calling the material a tutorial does not change the operational objective or the way participation is being cultivated.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference side treats the instructional label as dispositive, but the conduct described is promotional: attract product traffic, conceal the earning pitch from the ad, then expose visitors to affiliate prompts and post-purchase emails. The promise of templates and replication is not incidental commentary; it is a participation pathway. A disclaimer about success cannot undo that directed recruitment design.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The evidence supports an operational marketing tutorial, not concealment of a scam. The presenter says affiliate-program advertising is not allowed on Facebook and explains where permitted website prompts may appear; that is a platform-compliance instruction, not proof that the opportunity is fraudulent. He also warns against overdoing affiliate promotion, and the description states that success is not guaranteed.
